questions.prompt: Using the model for The Joule-Thomson Effect, Throttling, and Inversion Temperature, set up the governing equation, inequality, derivative, probability, or phase-rule count and solve the following problem: A gas with \(\mu_{JT}=2.5\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{K\,Pa^{-1}}\) undergoes an isenthalpic pressure change of \(\Delta p=-4.0\times10^6\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Estimate \(\Delta T\) while treating the coefficient as constant.
questions.answer:
Model:
Apply the model for The Joule-Thomson Effect, Throttling, and Inversion Temperature under every condition stated in the question; use SI units unless another unit is explicitly supplied.

Working:
Use the local form following equation \([4]\): \[\Delta T\simeq\mu_{JT}\Delta p=(2.5\times10^{-6})(-4.0\times10^6)\,\mathrm K=-10\,\mathrm K.\] The pressure falls and the positive coefficient gives cooling, exactly as the inversion sign rule requires. Final result: \(\Delta T\simeq-10\,\mathrm K\).

Final answer:
\(\Delta T\simeq-10\,\mathrm K\).

Check:
Substituting the result back into the defining relation reproduces the stated data to the quoted precision. The final unit follows from the equation, and the qualitative trend agrees with the model.

Does it cool?
questions.answer:
Model:
Apply the model for The Joule-Thomson Effect, Throttling, and Inversion Temperature under every condition stated in the question; use SI units unless another unit is explicitly supplied.

The device still obeys the isenthalpic condition in equation \([1]\). However, \(dp\lt 0\) and \(\mu_{JT}\lt 0\), so equation \([4]\) gives \(dT\gt 0\). The conclusion agrees with both the defining relation and the relevant limiting or qualitative behaviour of the model.
